TRADEMARK ASSIGNMENT AGREEMENT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Acme Corp

ASSIGNMENT DECLARATION
Jordan Alex Lee ("Assignor") is the owner of the trademark described as follows: the word mark ACME and design logo (the "Mark"), U.S. registration or application number: U.S. Reg. No. 1,234,567. Assignor hereby assigns and transfers to Acme Corp ("Assignee") all of Assignor's right, title, and interest in and to the Mark, together with the goodwill of the business connected with the use of and symbolized by the Mark. This assignment includes the goodwill of the business connected with the use of the Mark, and is not an assignment of the Mark alone, separate from that goodwill. Assignor agrees to sign any additional documents, and to cooperate with any further steps, reasonably requested by Assignee to confirm, record, or perfect this assignment, including recording it with the United States Patent and Trademark Office.

ASSIGNMENT MUST CARRY THE GOODWILL OF THE BUSINESS CONNECTED WITH THE MARK
Federal trademark law does not treat a mark as a piece of property that can be sold on its own, detached from the business it identifies. The statute states that a registered mark, or a mark for which an application has been filed, is assignable only with the goodwill of the business in which the mark is used, or with that part of the goodwill of the business connected with the use of and symbolized by the mark. This is why an assignment like this one for the word mark ACME and design logo is written to expressly transfer the goodwill of the business connected with the mark's use, alongside the mark itself, rather than transferring the mark by itself.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A registered mark or a mark for which an application to register has been filed shall be assignable with the good will of the business in which the mark is used, or with that part of the good will of the business connected with the use of and symbolized by the mark."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1060(a)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, assignment of marks — goodwill requirement (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1060)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the statutory condition on assignability — not a claim that the goodwill actually being transferred by the assignor to the assignee under this particular agreement is sufficient in fact or in law, which depends on the underlying business and transaction and is not resolved by this clause. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (15 U.S.C. § 1060(a)(1), first sentence); the companion clause below on intent-to-use applications quotes a second sentence of that same subsection (a)(1), and is not an independent source from this one. This is federal law that applies nationwide; it does not address any state's separate law on assignment of a state-registered or common-law mark, which is addressed in a separate clause below. This document is informational only and does not itself determine whether any specific transfer of the mark described on this sheet complies with this statute.

AN INTENT-TO-USE APPLICATION GENERALLY CANNOT BE ASSIGNED BEFORE USE IS SHOWN
The general goodwill-assignability rule has a specific statutory carve-out for an application filed on an intent-to-use basis. The statute states that no application to register a mark filed under the intent-to-use provision is assignable before the applicant either files an amendment converting the application to a use-based filing, or files the verified statement of use required to complete registration — except for an assignment to a successor to the business of the applicant, or the portion of that business to which the mark pertains, if that business is ongoing and existing. In other words, until use in commerce has actually been shown (or the application amended to reflect it), an intent-to-use application generally cannot be assigned to just any buyer; the only assignee the statute permits at that stage is a successor to the applicant's own ongoing business. If the word mark ACME and design logo is the subject of a pending intent-to-use application rather than an issued registration or a use-based application, this restriction, not the general rule above, controls whether this assignment from Jordan Alex Lee to Acme Corp is one the statute permits at this time.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Notwithstanding the preceding sentence, no application to register a mark under section 1051(b) of this title shall be assignable prior to the filing of an amendment under section 1051(c) of this title to bring the application into conformity with section 1051(a) of this title or the filing of the verified statement of use under section 1051(d) of this title, except for an assignment to a successor to the business of the applicant, or portion thereof, to which the mark pertains, if that business is ongoing and existing."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1060(a)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, assignment of marks — restriction on assigning an intent-to-use application before use is shown (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1060)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of a statutory restriction distinct from, and narrower than, the general goodwill-assignability rule in the companion clause above; both quotes come from the same statutory subsection, 15 U.S.C. § 1060(a)(1) (the first and second sentences of that subsection), and are not independent sources of each other. This clause does not determine whether the named assignee in fact qualifies as a successor to the assignor's ongoing business, which is a factual question outside this document's scope, nor does it resolve whether the particular filing being assigned is registered, use-based, or intent-to-use — that characterization depends on the actual USPTO filing. This is federal law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule.

"ASSIGNMENT IN GROSS" — THE CONSEQUENCE OF ASSIGNING A MARK WITHOUT THE GOODWILL IT SYMBOLIZES
The goodwill requirement described above is not just a drafting formality. When a mark is transferred without the goodwill of the business connected with its use — sometimes called an "assignment in gross" — the transfer falls outside what the statute makes assignable, and courts applying the Lanham Act have treated such a transfer as legally deficient: an assignment in gross can be held invalid, and the assignee can be denied the ability to claim the priority of the assignor's earlier registration date or earlier date of first use, meaning the assignee may be treated as if its own rights in the mark began only with its own, later use rather than stepping into the assignor's shoes. This is the reason this agreement expressly states, in the declaration below, that the goodwill of the business connected with the use of the word mark ACME and design logo is included in what Jordan Alex Lee is transferring to Acme Corp — that statement is directed at avoiding exactly this doctrine.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A registered mark or a mark for which an application to register has been filed shall be assignable with the good will of the business in which the mark is used, or with that part of the good will of the business connected with the use of and symbolized by the mark."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1060(a)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, assignment of marks — goodwill requirement (statutory basis for the assignment-in-gross doctrine) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1060)

Rather than fabricate a case citation or quote, this clause describes the doctrine's substance — that it is a widely recognized construction of the statutory goodwill requirement, consistent with that requirement's own text — without citing a specific case for it, and that description should be understood as this document's own characterization of a body of case law that was not independently checked source-by-source in this session. This is federal law that applies nationwide; it does not resolve whether the specific transfer described in this agreement in fact includes goodwill sufficient to avoid this doctrine, which depends on the underlying business and transaction.

A TRADEMARK ASSIGNMENT MUST BE IN WRITING
Unlike a trademark license, which the Lanham Act does not require to be in writing, an assignment of a registered mark or a pending application must be by an instrument in writing, duly executed. This is part of why a signed, written document like this one — rather than a verbal understanding — is what is needed to actually transfer Jordan Alex Lee's ownership of the word mark ACME and design logo to Acme Corp.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Assignments shall be by instruments in writing duly executed."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1060(a)(3) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, assignment of marks — writing requirement (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1060)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the writing requirement — not a claim about what specific form of signature (handwritten, scanned, or fully electronic under the federal E-SIGN Act or a state UETA-equivalent statute) satisfies "instrument in writing" in every circumstance, which this clause does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (15 U.S.C. § 1060(a)(3)); the companion recording clause below quotes a second sentence of that same subsection together with a separate subsection, (a)(4), and neither is an independent source from this one. This is federal law that applies nationwide; California's own state trademark statute imposes a parallel writing requirement for assignment of a state-registered mark, addressed in a separate clause below.

RECORDING A TRADEMARK ASSIGNMENT WITH THE USPTO
Federal law permits, but does not itself require, an assignment like this one to be recorded with the United States Patent and Trademark Office. Recording matters because of a specific consequence for not doing so: an assignment is void against a later, good-faith purchaser who pays valuable consideration for the same mark without notice of this assignment, unless this assignment is recorded with the USPTO within three months of its date, or before the date of that later purchase. Separately, the statute describes what recording itself establishes: an acknowledged assignment is prima facie evidence that it was executed, and when the assignment is recorded with the USPTO, that record is likewise made prima facie evidence of execution — evidence, in other words, that the document was signed, not a USPTO determination that the underlying transfer is legally valid, that it includes the goodwill the statute requires, or that Acme Corp's resulting title is free of competing claims. Recording this assignment of the word mark ACME and design logo from Jordan Alex Lee to Acme Corp is a step the parties can take with the USPTO; this document does not itself record anything.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "when the prescribed information reporting the assignment is recorded in the United States Patent and Trademark Office, the record shall be prima facie evidence of execution"
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1060(a)(3) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, assignment of marks — recording as prima facie evidence of execution (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1060)
  "An assignment shall be void against any subsequent purchaser for valuable consideration without notice, unless the prescribed information reporting the assignment is recorded in the United States Patent and Trademark Office within 3 months after the date of the assignment or prior to the subsequent purchase."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1060(a)(4) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, assignment of marks — three-month recording window against a subsequent purchaser (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1060)

This is federal law that applies nationwide; it does not resolve whether recording occurs for any particular signed copy of this agreement, which is a step the parties would need to take themselves and which this document does not track.

CALIFORNIA HAS ITS OWN, PARALLEL ASSIGNMENT STATUTE FOR STATE-REGISTERED MARKS
Separate from the federal Lanham Act, California's own trademark statute — the Model State Trademark Law — addresses assignment of a mark registered with the California Secretary of State. It uses the same basic structure as the federal statute: a mark and its state registration are assignable with the goodwill of the business in which the mark is used, or with that part of the goodwill of the business connected with the use of and symbolized by the mark; the assignment must be by a written, duly executed instrument; and an assignment is void against a subsequent purchaser for valuable consideration without notice unless it is recorded with the Secretary of State within three months of the assignment's date or before that later purchase. This state statute is a separate, independent legal source from the federal recording and goodwill rules described above, and applies on its own terms to a mark registered under California's state trademark statute, distinct from a federal USPTO registration or application.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Any mark and its registration hereunder shall be assignable with the good will of the business in which the mark is used, or with that part of the good will of the business connected with the use of and symbolized by the mark. Assignment shall be by instrument in writing duly executed and may be recorded with the secretary upon the payment of the recording fee payable to the secretary as set forth in subdivision (b) of Section 12193 of the Government Code, who, upon recording of the assignment, shall issue in the name of the assignee a new certificate for the remainder of the term of the registration or of the last renewal thereof. An assignment of any registration under this chapter shall be void as against any subsequent purchaser for valuable consideration without notice, unless it is recorded with the secretary within three months after the date thereof or prior to the subsequent purchase."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 14220(a) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), Model State Trademark Law, assignment of a state-registered mark (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=14220.)
